name: harbour
desc: Portable, xBase-compatible programming language and environment
why: An xBase dialect with a living dBASE lineage, a real old-school environment, though this formula is deprecated.

brief.what_it_is: Harbour is an open, free-software implementation of an xBase-compatible programming language, described as cross-platform, multi-threaded, object-oriented and scriptable. It ships as a compiler plus runtime libraries, with several UI and database backends, its own build system (hbmk2), and a collection of libraries and bindings for popular APIs. You write Harbour source (.prg files) and compile it into native apps for GNU/Linux, Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, BSD and other *nix systems. The bundled executables are harbour, hbmk2, hbpp, hbrun, hbformat, hbi18n, hbnetio, hbtest, hb3rdpat.hbs.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames Harbour as the free software successor to Clipper/xBase: backward compatible with Clipper/xBase code and 100% compatible with Clipper compilers, so existing xBase applications can run on modern platforms from one code base.
brief.how_it_works: The compiler turns Harbour source into C-level output that is then built with a C compiler, using Harbour's own make system (hbmk2, driven by .hbp/.hbc project files) to handle the build. Optional third-party components are wired in through HB_WITH_* environment variables. Native RDDs, SQL and ODBC support sit in the runtime, alongside JSON, SSL, TCP/IP and XML support and Console, TUI, GUI, service/daemon and web app targets.

brief.install_notes: Harbour is normally built from source (the README lists no Homebrew-specific steps). Requirements: a supported ANSI C compiler and GNU Make (3.81 recommended, 3.79 minimum). On Linux, Debian/Ubuntu and RPM-based distros need base packages such as git, gcc, binutils and bison-related tooling. Optional contribs (ncurses, slang, X11, cairo, curl, mysql, pgsql, odbc, qt5, etc.) each need their own -dev packages. On Windows, you need a C compiler on PATH (MSVC, MinGW, Borland, Pelles C, Watcom and others are listed); the README recommends Windows XP or later. Third-party dependencies are found automatically on *nix; on Windows, MS-DOS and OS/2 you set HB_WITH_* environment variables pointing at their headers. HB_BUILD_NOGPLLIB=yes disables GPL-dependent parts for closed-source use. No accounts or licence keys are needed.
brief.standout: Harbour carries a full xBase toolchain forward: its own compiler, its own build tool, a formatter, and runnable scripts, targeting an unusually wide range of platforms, from Windows CE, MS-DOS and OS/2 to iOS and Android. Its Clipper compatibility is the explicit selling point, which makes it a time capsule and a working modern environment at once.
brief.status: Maintained, by the evidence I could see. The homepage still says 'Latest stable: 3.0.0 (2011-07-17)' while the GitHub README says 'The latest official stable release is 3.2.0 (2026-07-07)', so the homepage is out of date. The README has five CI badges (linux, windows, macos, vm1, vm2), and it links to the GitHub commits feed. I did not see a last-commit date. The brew formula is described in the scout notes as deprecated, but I did not check the Homebrew formula itself.
brief.caveats: The README is long and was cut off at 40,000 characters, so I did not read the sections on troubleshooting, the platform matrix or the rest of the build examples. The homepage and README disagree on the current version. Builds depend on a C compiler and GNU make, and Windows builds have many compiler-specific setups. The README says spaces in directory names are not supported in the build path, and that 3rd-party packages must be in their vanilla install layout. Some components are GPL-dependent (HB_BUILD_NOGPLLIB disables them). The README's own guarantees section says the document comes with no warranty and that contributors are not liable. The brew formula is listed as deprecated by the scout notes, which the brew caveats field does not confirm.

judge.reason: Harbour makes the living Clipper/xBase lineage tangible: compile legacy-style database programs into native apps across platforms, an unusual time capsule worth exploring.

entry.title: Harbour
entry.tldr: A free, Clipper-compatible xBase compiler that turns .prg source into native apps, keeping the dBASE-era language alive on modern systems.
entry.deeper_look:
Harbour is a free-software implementation of the xBase language family, the line of database-centred languages that grew out of dBASE and Clipper. You write `.prg` source files and the compiler turns them into C-level output, which a C compiler then builds into a native program. The project describes itself as "multi-platform, multi-threading, object-oriented, scriptable", and says it is "100% compatible with Clipper compilers".

It exists so that old xBase applications can keep running. Clipper was a commercial DOS-era compiler, and a great deal of business software was written in it. Harbour lets that code move to current platforms from one code base. The listed targets run from MS-DOS and OS/2 to Linux, macOS, iOS and Android.

The install brings a whole toolchain. `harbour` is the compiler, `hbmk2` is the build tool driven by `.hbp` and `.hbc` project files, `hbrun` runs scripts, and `hbformat` tidies source. The runtime has native database drivers (RDDs), SQL and ODBC support, JSON, SSL, TCP/IP and XML, with console, text-UI, GUI, daemon and web targets.

The door it opens is a language design from before SQL servers were the default. Database tables, records and screen handling sit close to the core of the language, and a whole generation of software was built that way. Harbour is a working way to read and run it.

brew install harbour
# The Homebrew formula is marked deprecated. The upstream README builds from source and needs an ANSI C compiler and GNU Make.

entry.whats_unique: It carries a complete xBase toolchain forward, with its own compiler, build system, formatter and scripting runner, and keeps Clipper compatibility as its explicit goal. It is both a time capsule and a working modern environment.
